title: The acoustic storyteller
intro: Just a voice, a guitar and a harmonica. Start here to hear how fast he went from singing other people's songs to writing ones everybody else would sing.

stops.why: The debut is mostly traditional songs and blues. Only two originals made it on, one of them a tribute to Woody Guthrie.
try: The House of the Rising Sun

stops.why: A year later, almost all his own songs, and several that went round the world.
try: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right

stops.why: His most openly topical record: news stories and protest set to plain, hard folk arrangements.
Recorded in a single night in June 1964, and already turning away from protest towards more personal songs.
Publishing demos cut for his music publisher: rough first drafts of many of these songs, and some he never recorded properly.

title: Going electric
intro: Eighteen months that changed what a rock record could say. Bands, organ, long songs, and audiences who did not all approve.

stops.why: Electric on one side, acoustic on the other: the turn happens inside a single album.
Opens with Like a Rolling Stone and ends with the eleven-minute, acoustic Desolation Row.
A double album made mostly in Nashville, looser and stranger than anything before it.
Manchester, 17 May 1966. A quiet acoustic first half, then the Hawks, the heckles and a furious Like a Rolling Stone.
The studio sessions behind all of this: false starts, rehearsals and songs finding their shape.

title: Basement, barn and Nashville
intro: After the noise of 1966, a sudden step back: home recordings with the Band, spare country records and a new, smoother voice.

stops.why: Recorded with the Band in upstate New York in 1967, passed around for years, and only released officially in 1975.
Short, sparse songs made with a tiny Nashville band, at the height of psychedelia.
Full country, a crooning voice, and a duet with Johnny Cash.
Outtakes from those Nashville years, including the sessions with Johnny Cash.
A puzzling double album of covers, live tracks and instrumentals. Easier to love next to its companion, Another Self Portrait.

title: Blood, tracks and thunder
intro: A great songwriter at full strength again: one of his most loved albums, the sessions behind it, and the travelling circus that followed.

stops.why: Recorded in New York in September 1974; he re-cut five songs in Minneapolis that December before release.
The New York sessions as they first sounded: quieter, closer, often just voice and guitar.
Long story songs, Scarlet Rivera's violin and Emmylou Harris's harmonies.
try: One More Cup of Coffee (Valley Below)

stops.why: The Rolling Thunder Revue of autumn 1975: small halls, white face paint, a big band of friends.
The second leg in 1976, rougher and angrier, released straight after the tour.

title: The gospel years
intro: Three records and a run of tours about faith, with some of the hardest-working bands he ever led. Divisive at the time, and much reassessed since.

stops.why: Made at Muscle Shoals with Mark Knopfler on guitar. Gotta Serve Somebody won him a Grammy.
Fully gospel, with a choir of backing singers driving the songs.
Faith alongside other subjects again, and one of his finest late songs to close.
The live shows, where these songs sounded best.

title: The late masterpieces
intro: Blues, old popular song and long, dark ballads, made by a man in his late fifties to late seventies who sounded more at ease than ever.

stops.why: Produced by Daniel Lanois, swampy and haunted. It won the Grammy for Album of the Year.
Released on 11 September 2001: blues, swing and rockabilly with a grin.
His first US number one album since Desire, thirty years earlier.
Murder ballads and long tales, including a fourteen-minute song about the Titanic.
Released at 79. It closes with Murder Most Foul, a song of nearly seventeen minutes.
